🐐 Goats With Bound Udders — the halakha through several versions of the Rav-Shmuel dispute
🐫 New Mishna: How a Camel May NOT Go Out — akud, ragul, and tying camels in a line

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Definitions, a New Mishna, and a New Chapter's Themes
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 54a–54b
overview.hebrewSource: רַב אָמַר: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara finishes explaining the mishna's unusual terms for how ewes are bound and wrapped, then works through several versions of the halakhic dispute over binding a goat's udder. A new mishna opens describing what a camel and other animals may NOT wear on Shabbat — bound legs, a saddlecloth tied only to the tail, bells, ladders, and more — with the Gemara supplying the reason for nearly every item. The daf closes with a memorable string of failed guesses at the meaning of 'ḥanunot' and a teaching about the duty to protest wrongdoing, which sets up the next daf's extended discussion.

slides.title: 📖 Unpacking the Mishna's Terms for Ewes
slides.subtitle: Each term is traced to a biblical root
rows: Tails fastened up, to make mounting easier for the males
'Attire of a harlot' (Proverbs 7:10) — an acronym for exposure
Tails bound down, to prevent mounting
'Land of Kavul' (I Kings 9:13) — land that produces no fruit
Wrapped in cloth from birth to keep the wool fine
Compared to 'clean wool of a newborn lamb' used for a leprosy sign (mishna, Nega'im)

callout.label: Land of Kavul, two ways:
callout.text: Rav Huna: the people there were laden with silver and gold and idle; Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: it was simply sandy, unproductive soil.

slides.title: 🐐 The Evolving Halakha on Goats' Bound Udders
slides.subtitle: Several amoraim transmit the same dispute in different forms

steps.content: 1️⃣ As a dispute on the mishna itself: Rav rules like Rabbi Yehuda (permits binding to dry the milk); Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yosei (prohibits all binding)
2️⃣ As an independent teaching: Rav permits drying but not conserving; Shmuel prohibits both
3️⃣ As a teaching on the baraita itself: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira notes that in practice no one can tell which binding is which by sight, so both are prohibited
4️⃣ Final halakha (Rabbi Yoḥanan via Ravin): follows the first, unnamed tanna, who permits goats to go out with bound udders in all cases

callout.label: Why so many versions?
callout.text: The Gemara preserves each transmission because later amoraim disagreed about exactly how earlier ones had ruled — a common feature of halakhic transmission.

slides.title: 🐫 New Mishna: How a Camel May Not Be Tied
slides.subtitle: Binding an animal's legs, and pulling several camels in a line

nodes.content: 🚫 Akud: binding foreleg to hind leg (or two forelegs to two hind legs), 'like the binding of Isaac'
🚫 Ragul: bending the lower foreleg onto the upper leg and tying it, leaving only three usable legs
🚫 Tying several camels together and pulling the lead one — Rav Ashi: forbidden because it looks like heading to market (חִינְגָּא)
✅ Permitted: holding each camel's separate rope in hand and pulling them all — provided the ropes are not intertwined (a kilayim concern, wool with linen)

callout.label: Rope-length detail:
callout.text: Shmuel: no more than a handbreadth of rope may hang below the hand (a baraita says two); and the rope between camel and person must be raised at least a handbreadth off the ground.

slides.title: 🐔 More Forbidden Gear — and Its Purpose
slides.subtitle: The new mishna's second half, with the Gemara's reasons

boxes.title: Donkey / Rooster
items: Untied saddlecloth — might fall, might be carried back
Bell, even plugged — looks like heading to market
Ladder on the neck — used for a wound, but not everyday wear
Rooster's leg-strap/strings — an ownership mark, still forbidden

boxes.title: Ram / Calf / Cow
items: Small wagon under a ram's tail — protects the tail from dragging
Gimon on a calf — a small yoke to train it early
Hedgehog skin on a cow's udder — keeps creeping animals from suckling
Strap between a cow's horns — depends on the beauty-vs-securing dispute (Shabbat 52)

callout.label: Footnote:
callout.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's cow went out with a strap between its horns 'against the Sages' will' — but the Gemara later reveals it wasn't even his cow; it was his neighbor's, called by his name only because he failed to protest.

slides.title: 🌳 What Exactly Is 'Ḥanunot'?
slides.subtitle: Two proposals rejected as too luxurious before a third is accepted

lines.speaker: Rav Aḥa
lines.text: From shearing time, they soak wool in oil and place it on the ewe's forehead so she won't catch cold.

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda
lines.text: If so, you've turned her into the Exilarch, Mar Ukva! Too pampering for a sheep.

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel
lines.text: At birthing time, two oil-soaked wool pieces are placed on her forehead and womb, to warm her.

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman
lines.text: Then you've made her into Yalta! Also too luxurious.

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: A wood chip from the ḥanun tree is placed in her nose to induce sneezing, expelling head-worms — hence 'ḥanunot,' merciful treatment.

callout.label: Accepted:
callout.text: The name reflects genuine mercy shown to the animal, not indulgence.

summary.principle: The mishna's unusual terms for tying and binding animals each describe a real practical purpose — from preventing mounting to easing a wound — and the new mishna forbids only bindings that risk falling off or that carry inappropriate appearances, like heading to market.

flowSteps.content: 📖 Sheḥuzot, kevulot, kevunot: each term traced to a biblical root describing tail-binding or wool-care
🐐 Final halakha on goats' udders: permitted in all cases, following the first tanna

columns.content: 🐫 New mishna: akud, ragul, and market-style camel trains are all forbidden
🐔 Bells, ladders, wagons, and hedgehog skin each serve — or fail to serve — a real animal need

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whoever can protest wrongdoing and does not becomes implicated in it — from one's household to the whole world

quiz.q: What is the halakhic conclusion (per Rabbi Yoḥanan, as transmitted by Ravin) regarding goats going out with bound udders?
o: It is always prohibited
It is permitted in all cases, following the first, unnamed tanna
It depends on the goat's owner
It is permitted only on weekdays
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes that when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported that Rabbi Yoḥanan ruled in accordance with the first tanna, who permits binding a goat's udder in all circumstances.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda's explanation, what does 'akud' mean in the new mishna about camels?
o: Tying two forelegs together only
Binding a foreleg to a hind leg, similar to the binding of Isaac
Placing a saddle without a strap
Leading several camels in a chain
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda explains that akud refers to binding a foreleg and a hind leg together, likened to the akeidah, the binding of Isaac.

quiz.q: Why does Rav Ashi say it is forbidden to tie several camels together and pull the lead one?
o: Because it constitutes a forbidden mixture (kilayim)
Because it makes the owner appear as though heading to market to sell or deliver merchandise
Because camels cannot be tied to each other under any circumstances
Because it causes the camels pain
quiz.e: Rav Ashi explains the concern is one of appearance (mechzei): tying camels in a train and pulling them makes the owner look like he is going to market, which is inappropriate on Shabbat.

quiz.q: What was ultimately revealed about the ownership of the cow that went out with a strap between its horns, associated with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya?
o: It genuinely belonged to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
It belonged to his neighbor, and was called by his name only because he failed to protest her practice
It was a wild, ownerless cow
It belonged to the Sages collectively
quiz.e: A baraita reveals the cow was not his but his neighbor's; because he did not protest her conduct, it was attributed to him — to his discredit.

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna's accepted explanation, what does 'ḥanunot' refer to regarding ewes?
o: Oil-soaked wool placed on the forehead against cold
Two oil pouches placed at birthing time
A wood chip from the ḥanun tree placed in the nose to induce sneezing and expel head-worms
A jeweled ornament for wealthy owners' flocks
quiz.e: After two more indulgent suggestions were rejected as too luxurious for a sheep, Rav Huna's explanation — a chip from the ḥanun tree inducing a sneeze that expels worms — was accepted, fitting the term's meaning of showing mercy.
